what: This project was a heritage digital twin web app developed for Blenheim Palace to support long-term conservation planning. The aim was to build an interactive 3D model of the palace that could incorporate IoT sensor data and reported incidents or survey results, helping to highlight areas at risk due to environmental or structural factors. By integrating multiple sources of data into a spatially accurate model, the platform enables conservation staff to assess conditions and prioritise interventions more effectively. The work was done in collaboration with a geosciences researcher from the University of Oxford and represents an innovative application of digital twin technology in the heritage sector.
why: I was particularly excited by the challenge of building what could be the first digital twin platform specifically designed for heritage conservation. The opportunity to contribute to something so cutting-edge, especially in a domain where this kind of technology is rarely applied, was highly motivating. I also enjoyed working with IoT data and building something that had the potential to make a real impact in how historic sites are maintained. Collaborating with a geosciences researcher from Oxford University added depth and a strong interdisciplinary dimension to the project.
how: As the full-stack developer, I built a REST API using Express and Node.js to handle survey and incident data, and designed a responsive front-end interface using React. The 3D model of Blenheim Palace was integrated with CesiumJS, allowing users to explore the site visually and see data overlays linked to different parts of the structure. Features include tools for reporting incidents, viewing metadata, filtering by location or time, and managing application state. I also set up a CI/CD workflow to streamline development and ensure smooth deployment of updates.
outcome: The project is ongoing. A working prototype is in place, with core functionality for reporting, data visualisation, and interactive exploration already developed. Remaining milestones include incorporating live IoT sensor data and building a timescale visualisation of changes across the site. Once completed, the app will provide a pioneering platform for digital heritage management and conservation planning.
